title: Will You Leave Nu'm’s People at Daybreak?
intro: Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a recalls a night visit to Nu'm at Dhu Dawran. Nu'm and her friend Asma first wonder whether the weather-beaten traveller can really be the man they know. When he has to leave the waking camp, Nu'm’s sisters take charge of his escape. Al-Baghdadi records a tradition that Umar recited the poem to Ibn Abbas. Its final adventure belongs to a thirsty camel at a lonely well.

translation: Will you leave Nu'm’s people early in the morning,
tomorrow at daybreak, or later, in the midday heat?
1.sharh: He speaks to himself as a traveller choosing his hour of departure. Each time of day comes with its own verb for setting out.

translation: all for a heart’s desire you never spoke of when asked,
to offer an excuse? A word can give you one.
2.sharh: He has kept the reason for his departure to himself. Abd al-Hamid understands the question as addressed to the traveller throughout. A few words in reply to those who asked might have excused him.

translation: You wander after Nu'm. There is no coming together,
no cord to join you, and your heart will not desist.
3.sharh: The scattered company and the severed cord are two ways of seeing the separation. His own heart is the one thing he cannot bring to a stop.

translation: Her nearness does you no good when she draws close.
Distance brings no solace, and you cannot bear it.
4.sharh: Near her he still cannot have his wish. Far away he has the same desire and no relief for it.

translation: Something else stands between you and Nu'm. Its like
would check a prudent man, if you would pause and think.
5.sharh: He leaves the new obstacle unnamed for a moment. A man with his wits about him, he tells himself, would already have turned back.

translation: Whenever I visit Nu'm, there is always a kinsman
of hers who bares his teeth each time we meet.
6.sharh: The obstacle now has a face. Every visit brings him up against a relative who takes on a tiger’s ferocity.

translation: It galls him that I should call at her house.
He nurses rancour against me and lets his hatred show.
7.sharh: Even a brief call offends the kinsman. Umar distinguishes the enmity the man carries inside him from what is plain in his manner.

translation: Carry my greeting to her, for a visit from me
would be made the talk of everyone and frowned upon.
8.sharh: He turns to a messenger who can do what the lover cannot do openly. An ordinary visit from him would bring talk and blame on the household.

translation: Give her this sign, what she said the morning we met
where the waters run out at Aknan. “Is this the famous man?
9.sharh: The messenger has a private means of identification, the very words used at their meeting. Umar recalls Nu'm sighting him where a watercourse emerges at Aknan.

translation: Stop and look, Asma. Do you recognise him?
Is this the man of al-Mughira’s house people talked of?
10.sharh: Nu'm asks Asma to put a name to the passer-by. The family name points to Umar through his ancestor al-Mughira.

translation: Is this the man you praised to me so highly?
By your life, I could never forget him until my burial.”
11.sharh: Asma’s glowing description has already fixed him in her friend’s memory. Nu'm swears by Asma’s life that the impression will last the length of her own.

translation: She said, “Yes, surely. What has changed his colour
is riding hard through the night and travelling at noon.”
12.sharh: Asma can account for the face that looks so different. He keeps his mount going through the dark and is still on the road in the heat of the day.

translation: “If it is really he, he has changed since we parted
from the man we knew. People do change.”
13.sharh: The women recognise a difference even as they settle his identity. The last few words sound like something one friend might say to the other to account for it.

translation: She saw a man who, when the sun stood across his path,
took its full glare, and in the evening went cold.
14.sharh: He fills out what the women could see in his face. There was nowhere on that journey to escape either the sun or the evening chill.

translation: A man at home on the road, crossing country, tossed
from waste to waste until his hair and clothes are dust.
15.sharh: Travel is a constant companion. The deserts take the active part, throwing him from one to the next until the journeys show on his body.

translation: How little shade he has on his mount’s back,
apart from what his striped cloak keeps off him.
16.sharh: Riding high leaves him exposed. His patterned cloak is the whole extent of the shelter he carries with him.

translation: What pleases her in her own life is a shaded chamber
and a green, well-watered tangle of gardens,
17.sharh: The view shifts indoors and then out to the adjoining gardens. Both the shade and the dense growth imply water and shelter close at hand.

translation: and someone to see to everything that concerns her.
Nothing keeps her awake late into the night.
18.sharh: Someone else has assumed the business of keeping her comfortable. Her untroubled sleep brings us back to his long hours of night riding.

translation: One night at Dhu Dawran, longing drove me to ride on.
A lover who hazards his life will shoulder terror.
19.sharh: Dhu Dawran gives the remembered adventure a place. He treats fear as a burden a lover can choose to shoulder.

translation: I spent the night watching the camp, on the brink,
wary of anyone on the rounds, looking towards them
20.sharh: His watch puts him in danger the whole time. The brink can be pictured as an actual edge, but Abd al-Hamid takes it as the nearness of disaster. He keeps his eyes on the men who might be making rounds.

translation: to see when sleep would have them in its grip.
A rough seat mine would be, were it not for my desire.
21.sharh: He must wait for sleep to take everyone. The ground on which he has chosen to sit would be intolerable without the prospect that keeps him there.

translation: My young camel spent the night in the open, her saddle
lying exposed to any night visitor who might come by.
22.sharh: He cannot hover near the camel and still keep his watch. Anyone coming through after dark could help himself to the saddle.

translation: I spent the night asking myself, “Where is her tent?
How am I to find a way out of what I am doing?”
23.sharh: The questions look forward and back along his intended route. He has still to find her tent, let alone work out how to leave it.

translation: My heart found the way to her by a scent I knew
as hers, and a desire in me that all but showed itself.
24.sharh: What he cannot yet see he recognises by scent. Desire itself becomes a guide, strong enough to threaten his concealment.

translation: When I ceased to hear a sound from them and out went
the lamps and little fires they had lit that evening,
25.sharh: He takes stock one sense at a time. The darkening camp is a piece of evidence alongside the silence he has been listening for.

translation: when the little moon whose setting I longed for sank,
the herdsmen came home and the late talkers fell asleep,
26.sharh: Even the little moon was too much light. He counts the return of the last people from the pastures, then the silence of those who stay up talking.

translation: and the voices around me died low, I came stealing
like a snake, my body aslant for fear of the camp.
27.sharh: The name of the creature arrives after the verse break. His sidelong posture makes sense of the snake’s quiet, gliding walk.

translation: I greeted her. Taken by surprise, she lost her wits
and nearly cried aloud in answer to my whispered greeting.
28.sharh: The sound he had tried hardest to avoid almost comes from Nu'm herself. His voice has been low, but the surprise threatens to make hers ring out.

translation: Biting her fingertips, she said, “You have disgraced me.
Even the easiest thing about you is hard to bear.
29.sharh: Her gesture precedes her reckoning of the risk. What he may have found easy to do has put her good name in danger.

translation: Tell me, even if we count for little with you, weren’t you afraid?
May you be kept safe. There are enemies here all round me.
30.sharh: She can scold and wish him safe in the same breath. Whatever price he puts on the women’s safety, he has also ventured among men hostile to him.

translation: By God, I cannot tell. Was it some pressing desire
that brought you by night, or is the man you feared asleep?”
31.sharh: Each possibility offers a different explanation of his timing. The second comes close to the precautions he took while she was unaware of him.

translation: I told her, “Longing and love brought me
to you. Not a soul knows of it.”
32.sharh: He can answer about his own desire with certainty. His assurance about everyone else in the camp is a much bolder claim.

translation: She softened. When her fright had lifted, she said,
“May your Lord Most High keep watch over you.
33.sharh: Her fear leaves her and her manner changes with it. She entrusts his safety to a greater keeper than the adventurer himself.

translation: Abu al-Khattab, no one will dispute it with you.
You shall have command of me for as long as you stay.”
34.sharh: Nu'm uses his familiar byname and gives him command for the duration of his visit. The morning will find her the one best able to direct what happens.

translation: What a night. All its length shrank away.
My nights before that one were never short.
35.sharh: Waiting had measured out the darkness hour by hour. In Nu'm’s company the very same stretch of night seems to slip away.

translation: What delight there was, what a place to sit
together, with no one to trouble us.
36.sharh: The repeated sounds in the Arabic dwell on the disturbance that never came. For those hours the two have the place to themselves.

translation: Her mouth breathes out the keenest musk,
her front teeth clean, their edges finely notched.
37.sharh: He approaches the mouth through scent, then sees the shapes of the teeth. Their fine ridges and edges give detail to the more general praise of whiteness.

translation: When the lips draw back, what you see is like
hailstones, or daisies in flower.
38.sharh: The comparison waits for her smile. Hail supplies separate bright pellets and the daisy a white flower newly opened.

translation: She gazes at me as a wild calf gazes
at a gazelle in the middle of a thicket.
39.sharh: The gaze is sustained and quiet. It opens a little space of foliage and watching animals inside the telling of the night encounter.

translation: When all but a little of the night had gone
and the last of its stars were about to sink,
40.sharh: At the beginning, the setting moon was his signal to approach. The last stars now tell him that his time with her is nearly up.

translation: she signalled that it was time for the camp
to stir. “Let our next meeting be at Azwar.”
41.sharh: With the camp about to wake she has to signal. The place she names keeps open the possibility of another meeting even as this one ends.

translation: What startled me was a caller crying, “Break camp!”
A familiar red streak of dawn had appeared.
42.sharh: A human cry breaks the silence he worked so hard to secure. The first reddish light is already enough for the camp to begin its departure.

translation: When she saw who had stirred among them
and who was wide awake, she said, “What do you advise?”
43.sharh: She takes stock of exactly how far the waking has gone. Their conversation has to become a practical discussion of how he can leave.

translation: “I will go out and face them. Either I get away
or the sword will find a wrong to avenge and avenge it.”
44.sharh: His plan gives him just two outcomes, flight or a sword drawn for vengeance. It does little to protect Nu'm from the consequences of being found with him.

translation: She said, “Would you prove what a spiteful man has said
against us and make the stories people tell come true?
45.sharh: A hostile man’s tale and a story passed from mouth to mouth would suddenly have a witness. She sees the damage in producing that witness himself.

translation: If something must be done, some other course
will come closer to secrecy and give you better cover.
46.sharh: She accepts the urgency. What she asks him to change is the means of leaving, so that his departure can be as discreet as his arrival.

translation: I shall tell my two sisters how our business began.
I have no room left to put off letting them know.
47.sharh: She will take her sisters into her confidence and tell the whole story. Telling two people deliberately is now her best chance to keep the rest from finding out.

translation: Perhaps they can find you a way out
and their hearts take in what has left mine so straitened.”
48.sharh: She pictures courage as space in the chest. Her sisters may have room to consider calmly what has left her scarcely able to breathe or think.

translation: She rose distraught, the blood gone from her face
with grief, letting a tear roll down.
49.sharh: The memory settles on two changes in her face, the blood ebbing away and one tear moving down. She has still to make her confession.

translation: Two freeborn women rose to meet her, wearing
two silk cloaks, one of fine white silk and one green.
50.sharh: The sisters enter as two distinct figures, one in pale silk and one in green. Clothing will shortly give them the means of bringing him out.

translation: She said to her sisters, “Help me look after a man
who came visiting. One thing is appointed for another.”
51.sharh: She presents the stranger as a visitor in need of their help. Her appeal to the way events are ordained softens the account of how he came to be there.

translation: They came up in alarm, then both said,
“Spare yourself the blame. It is easier than you think.”
52.sharh: Their alarm is brief. Once they have seen the situation they can offer the reassurance their sister had hoped for.

translation: The younger told her, “I’ll give him my outer wrap
and my shift, and this striped cloak if he’s afraid.
53.sharh: The younger sister can supply the disguise herself. She thinks through its layers, from a woman’s shift out to a conspicuous striped cloak.

translation: He can get up and walk in disguise between us.
Our secret will stay safe and he will go unseen.”
54.sharh: His place in the group matters as much as the clothes. A figure walking between the women gives an onlooker no obvious reason to look again.

translation: So my shield against the men I feared
was three young women, two grown and one just coming of age.
55.sharh: He had imagined his way out with a sword. The shield that actually protects him is formed by Nu'm and her two sisters walking round him.

translation: When we had crossed the open space of the camp they said,
“Have you no fear of enemies when the night is moonlit?
56.sharh: They wait until the exposed ground is behind them before speaking. Their question makes him see the visit from the point of view of those who had to get him safely out.

translation: “Is this how you always go on, heedless?
Have you no shame? Won’t you stop and think?
57.sharh: The women widen their reproach from one night to a habit. Their quick succession of questions echoes his own appeal to his better judgement at the opening.

translation: “When you come, let your eyes rest on someone else,
so they will think your love lies where you look.”
58.sharh: Their last piece of advice concerns the next visit. He can enlist the watchers’ own way of reasoning by allowing them to follow his gaze to the wrong person.

translation: My last sight of her was when she turned aside
and a clear cheek and the curve of an eye showed.
59.sharh: She turns away and for an instant he still has her profile. The outline of the eye and the light cheek are the details that stay with him.

translation: Though I did say one thing to her, “Nu'm,”
as the fine camels of Arhab were being urged on,
60.sharh: The visual memory draws one last spoken exchange after it. He has time for a word as the caravan camels are already being called forward.

translation: “Happy the people of the woman of Amir, with her sweet
scent about them, the fragrance I remember.”
61.sharh: Her people will go on living within reach of the scent he can now only remember. Earlier, it had guided him in the dark.

translation: I went to my full-grown camel, whose fat had wasted away
on the night rides, till even her flesh had worn thin,
62.sharh: His attention returns to the animal he left in the open. Her wasting body has kept as exact an account of the journeys as his weathered face.

translation: and so had my keeping her waiting on my errands, till she was
a sliver of plank, or a travelling frame lashed together.
63.sharh: The delays of his visit have cost her as much as the riding. In place of flesh he sees a bare wooden structure and its tight bindings.

translation: There was a waterhole in an all but unvisited waste,
in open tracts where no summer camp had gathered.
64.sharh: The long description begins by naming the water. Even in summer, when people gather at permanent wells, there is no camp beside this one.

translation: A spider had built there. Across the edges
it looked like a raw hide spread out.
65.sharh: The web spans the rim like a raw hide laid out flat. No frequent coming and going has broken it.

translation: I came to it without knowing whether the night
still ahead of me was longer than the part already gone.
66.sharh: Only now does the verb of arrival complete the sentence about the waterhole. He cannot even tell which side of midnight he has reached.

translation: I turned to my long-striding camel. When she glanced round
there was something mad in the way she looked.
67.sharh: The animal that once covered ground with long strides is now staring wildly about. The water is close enough for thirst to undo her good sense.

translation: In her eagerness for water she wrested her head against me.
Between her and what she wanted lay a dangerous well.
68.sharh: She feels the pull of the water and he feels it at the other end of the rein. The open well makes her very eagerness a danger to her.

translation: She kept trying for the water. But for her halter
and my pulling her back, she would have broken her bones over and over.
69.sharh: Her rushes come in bursts. A piece of tack and the rider’s arm are all that keep a thirsty beast from falling down the shaft.

translation: When I saw her plight, and saw that I was
in a stretch of country with nowhere to turn for help,
70.sharh: He has assessed both the animal’s distress and the country about them. No one else will rig the means of getting the water to her.

translation: I marked off part of the trough and made her a fresh basin,
about a handspan wide, if that.
71.sharh: He sections off a tiny part along the side of the trough. Its size is something he can measure on his own hand.

translation: Once she put her mouth to it, there was scarcely
a palm’s breadth of water left over beside her lips.
72.sharh: The basin is measured a second time against the camel’s mouth. Her broad lips occupy almost the whole patch of water he has contrived for her.

translation: I had no bucket but a wooden bowl. Its well rope
was a camel strap and a length of plaited leather.
73.sharh: He now tells how he raised water from below. A drinking bowl and the leather of his travelling gear have to serve as bucket and well rope.

translation: She sniffed it without turning away, and drank
her fill, undeterred by the cloudy water beasts had trodden.
74.sharh: The camel gets the last action. However uninviting the water smelt or looked after other animals had disturbed it, she drank on until her thirst was gone.

1.1.3.head: نُعم
1.1.3.meaning: Nu'm, the woman whom Umar visits. He calls her a woman of Amir near the end.

1.2.5.head: مُهَجِّر
1.2.5.meaning: Travelling in the heat of midday.

2.2.1.head: أَبلَغَ
2.2.1.meaning: To convey an excuse. The reciter appears to say fa-mubligha. The diwan and studio card have the verb fa-tubligha, which completes the preceding negative clause.

3.1.5.head: الشَّمل
3.1.5.meaning: The company of people gathered together, here the lovers’ reunion.

3.2.2.head: الحَبل
3.2.2.meaning: The bond that holds two people together, pictured as a cord.

3.2.6.head: مُقصِر
3.2.6.meaning: Desisting, as a heart might give up its pursuit.

4.2.3.head: أَسلى
4.2.3.meaning: To bring forgetfulness or relief from the ache of remembering.

5.2.2-3.head: ذو النُّهى
5.2.2-3.meaning: “A man of judgement”, someone whose understanding keeps him from rashness.

5.2.5.head: اِرعَوى
5.2.5.meaning: To draw back or come to one’s senses.

6.2.4.head: تَنَمَّرَ
6.2.4.meaning: To turn fierce on someone, likened to a tiger.

8.1.1.meaning: Carry my message, act as my messenger.

8.2.2.head: إِلمام
8.2.2.meaning: A visit or passing call at someone’s home.

9.1.1.head: آيَة
9.1.1.meaning: A private token by which she can recognise his messenger.

9.2.1-2.head: مَدفَع أَكنان
9.2.1-2.meaning: Madfa' Aknan, the outlet of a watercourse at Aknan.

9.2.4.head: المُشَهَّر
9.2.4.meaning: The man whose name has been on everyone’s lips.

10.1.3.head: أَسماء
10.1.3.meaning: Asma, Nu'm’s companion, whom she asks to identify the passer-by.

10.2.2.head: المُغيرِيّ
10.2.2.meaning: Al-Mughiri, Umar’s family designation through his ancestor al-Mughira of Makhzum.

11.2.1.head: عَيش
11.2.1.meaning: “By your life”, an oath sworn by the life of the woman addressed.

12.2.4.head: نَصّ
12.2.4.meaning: Pressing a mount to a hard pace.

13.1.5.meaning: To have changed from a former state.

14.2.1.head: ضَحِيَ
14.2.1.meaning: To stand exposed to the sun and its heat.

14.2.4.head: خَصِرَ
14.2.4.meaning: To feel the cold, here the evening chill after exposure to the sun.

15.1.3-4.head: جَوّاب أَرض
15.1.3-4.meaning: “A crosser of country”, a habitual far traveller.

16.1.1.head: قَليل
16.1.1.meaning: In the accusative it continues the description of the traveller she saw. The printed nominative makes a fresh statement, “little is his shade”.

16.2.6.head: المُحَبَّر
16.2.6.meaning: Patterned or striped, said of cloth.

17.2.1.head: رَيّان
17.2.1.meaning: Well-watered and luxuriant, describing the grounds around her.

18.1.1.head: والٍ
18.1.1.meaning: Someone who looks after her affairs.

19.1.2-3.head: ذو دَوران
19.1.2-3.meaning: Dhu Dawran, the place that gives its name to the night of the visit.

19.1.4.head: جَشَّمَ
19.1.4.meaning: Made me undertake a hardship. Longing is understood as what drove him out.

19.2.5.head: المُغَرِّر
19.2.5.meaning: One who puts himself at risk.

20.1.5.meaning: A brink or precipice, understood by the commentator as the danger of imminent discovery.

21.2.4.head: اللُّبانَة
21.2.4.meaning: A pressing desire or errand, here the meeting with Nu'm.

21.2.5.head: أَوعَر
21.2.5.meaning: Rough and uncomfortable underfoot or as a seat.

22.2.1-2.head: طارِق لَيل
22.2.1-2.meaning: Someone who arrives or passes through after dark.

22.2.6.head: مُعوِر
22.2.6.meaning: Exposed and unguarded. A passer-by could take the saddle.

23.1.5.head: خِباء
23.1.5.meaning: A tent of hair or wool, the private dwelling he seeks.

23.2.6.head: مَصدَر
23.2.6.meaning: A way out or a return, as when departing from a waterhole.

25.2.3-4.head: العِشاء
25.2.3-4.meaning: At nightfall, when the people of the camp lit their lamps. The printed texts use a different preposition for the same time of day.

25.2.5.head: أَنؤُر
25.2.5.meaning: Fires. This less familiar plural suggests the separate campfires.

26.1.2.head: قُمَير
26.1.2.meaning: A little moon. The diminutive makes even this scant light conspicuous.

26.2.1-2.head: رَوَّحَ الرِّعيان
26.2.1-2.meaning: The herdsmen came home with their animals towards evening.

26.2.4.head: سُمَّر
26.2.4.meaning: People who stay up talking after dark.

27.2.1.head: الحُباب
27.2.1.meaning: A snake, evoked for its noiseless, gliding movement.

27.2.5.head: أَزوَر
27.2.5.meaning: Bent or turned to one side as he moves.

28.1.4.head: تَوَلَّهَ
28.1.4.meaning: To lose one’s composure in a sudden fright.

29.2.3-4.head: مَيسور الأَمر
29.2.3-4.meaning: “The easy part of your business”, something which brings her difficulty all the same.

30.1.1.meaning: “Tell me”, introducing a question charged with reproach.

30.2.1.meaning: “May you be kept safe”, a blessing amid the rebuke.

31.2.1-2.head: سَرى
31.2.1-2.meaning: Carried you out by night, as desire is imagined doing.

33.1.4-5.head: أَفرَخَ رَوعُهُ
33.1.4-5.meaning: “Her fright cleared”, an idiom for fear leaving someone.

33.2.1.head: كَلا
33.2.1.meaning: May he guard you. The hamza of the verb kala'a is lightened.

34.1.2-3.head: أَبو الخَطّاب
34.1.2-3.meaning: Abu al-Khattab, a byname by which Nu'm addresses Umar.

34.2.5.head: مُؤَمَّر
34.2.5.meaning: Given command, here for the duration of his stay.

36.1.4.head: مَلهى
36.1.4.meaning: A pleasure or a place of enjoyment.

37.1.1.head: مَجَّ
37.1.1.meaning: To send out from the mouth, here a breath of musk.

37.1.5.head: مُقَبَّل
37.1.5.meaning: The place of a kiss, her mouth.

37.2.4.head: غُروب
37.2.4.meaning: The sharp outlines or fine edges of the teeth.

37.2.5.head: مُؤَشَّر
37.2.5.meaning: Finely notched along the edges of the teeth.

38.1.4.meaning: To part, as lips do in a smile.

38.2.4.head: أُقحُوان
38.2.4.meaning: A white daisy-like flower traditionally compared to bright teeth.

39.2.5.head: جُؤذَر
39.2.5.meaning: The calf of a wild cow, watching a gazelle.

40.2.2-3.head: تَوالي النُّجوم
40.2.2-3.meaning: The last stars in the succession to set.

41.2.5.head: عَزوَر
41.2.5.meaning: Azwar, a place the commentary locates in the region of al-Juhfa.

42.2.3.head: مَعروف
42.2.3.meaning: A recognisable sign of approaching dawn.

42.2.6.head: أَشقَر
42.2.6.meaning: Reddish, the tint in the first light on the horizon.

44.1.2.head: بادى
44.1.2.meaning: To come out openly before them.

44.2.4.head: ثَأر
44.2.4.meaning: Blood vengeance, here attributed to the sword itself.

45.2.5.head: أَثَرَ
45.2.5.meaning: Passed on as a report from someone else.

47.2.6.head: مُتَأَخَّر
47.2.6.meaning: Leeway to hold back or delay.

48.2.3.head: صَدر
48.2.3.meaning: She hopes her sisters will have the composure to think of a way out. The diwan and both anthologies read sirb, the mind or disposition.

48.2.6.head: حَصِرَ
48.2.6.meaning: To feel hemmed in and unable to see a way out.

49.2.3-4.head: أَذرى عَبرَةً
49.2.3-4.meaning: To shed a tear of grief.

50.2.3.head: خَزّ
50.2.3.meaning: A costly fabric made with silk.

50.2.4.head: دِمَقس
50.2.4.meaning: Fine white silk, describing one sister’s wrap.

52.2.4.head: الخَطب
52.2.4.meaning: A grave matter or alarming turn of events.

53.1.5.head: مِطرَف
53.1.5.meaning: An outer wrap with a border or stripe.

53.2.1.head: دِرع
53.2.1.meaning: A woman’s shift, worn under her outer clothing.

53.2.3.head: البُرد
53.2.3.meaning: A striped cloak or wrapping garment.

54.1.4.head: مُتَنَكِّر
54.1.4.meaning: Disguised so that an observer cannot pick him out.

55.1.2.head: مِجَنّ
55.1.2.meaning: My shield, the three women who screen him from view.

55.2.3.head: كاعِب
55.2.3.meaning: Two young women who have reached maturity.

55.2.4.head: مُعصِر
55.2.4.meaning: A girl just coming of age.

56.1.2.head: أَجازَ
56.1.2.meaning: To pass right through a place.

58.1.4-5.head: طَرف العَين
58.1.4-5.meaning: The direction of a glance, watched by anyone trying to discover his love.

59.2.5.head: مَحجِر
59.2.5.meaning: The socket and visible outline of the eye.

60.2.3.head: الأَرحَبِيّات
60.2.3.meaning: Arhabi camels, a prized breed associated with Arhab of Hamdan in Yemen.

61.1.3.head: العامِرِيَّة
61.1.3.meaning: The woman of Amir, his name for Nu'm here.

61.1.4.head: نَشر
61.1.4.meaning: A scent diffusing through the air.

62.1.4-5.meaning: “Ate away at her fat”, the gradual cost of the night journeys.

62.2.5.head: مُتَحَسِّر
62.2.5.meaning: Drawn away through wasting, exposing the frame.

63.2.4.head: شِجار
63.2.4.meaning: A wooden riding frame, smaller than a howdah.

64.2.1.head: بَسابِس
64.2.1.meaning: Broad stretches of open level country.

64.2.6.head: مَحضَر
64.2.6.meaning: A summer encampment by a settled water supply.

65.2.3.head: الأَرجاء
65.2.3.meaning: The sides and edges, here the rim of the well.

65.2.4.head: خام
65.2.4.meaning: A raw, untanned hide, the commentator’s gloss for the material evoked by the web.

66.1.1.head: وَرَدَ
66.1.1.meaning: To come to water for a drink. The verb completes the sentence opened two verses earlier.

67.1.3-4.head: مِغلاة أَرض
67.1.3-4.meaning: A camel whose stride covers ground quickly.

68.2.5.head: قَليب
68.2.5.meaning: A well or well shaft in the open country.

68.2.6.head: مُعَوَّر
68.2.6.meaning: A damaged or unsafe well, dangerous to an animal straining towards it.

69.1.4.head: زِمام
69.1.4.meaning: The rein by which a camel is led or held back.

70.2.5.head: مُعَصَّر
70.2.5.meaning: A refuge or place to turn for help.

71.1.1.head: قَصَرَ
71.1.1.meaning: To confine or mark off a small section along the trough.

71.2.2-3.head: قاب الشِّبر
71.2.2-3.meaning: About a handspan, thumb to little finger.

72.1.2.head: شَرَعَ
72.1.2.meaning: To reach into water to drink.

72.2.3-4.head: قِدى الكَفّ
72.2.3-4.meaning: The measure or breadth of the palm.

73.1.4.head: القَعب
73.1.4.meaning: A stout drinking bowl, used here as a bucket.

73.2.3.head: نِسع
73.2.3.meaning: A leather strap used for securing a camel’s saddle or load.

73.2.4-5.head: الأَديم المُضَفَّر
73.2.4-5.meaning: Tanned leather plaited into a strong line.

74.1.1.head: سافَ
74.1.1.meaning: To sniff, as the camel does before drinking.

74.1.3.head: عافَ
74.1.3.meaning: To turn from something in distaste.

74.2.3.head: مَطروق
74.2.3.meaning: Water visited and disturbed by other beasts.
